113.title: Watching change
113.hook: steps thirteen to sixteen: impermanence, fading, ceasing, letting go
113.howItsDone: In Buddhist breath meditation, the final steps turn attention to impermanence, the fading of attachment, ending and letting go, and many teachers use the breath's endings as the doorway.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gladdening the mind: known, gladdened, steadied, set free. Your line was release. Did you loosen a grip today? Day one hundred and thirteen, and the last four steps.

Try something. Listen to the next sound you hear. A car, a fridge, a bird. Listen until it stops. Notice the exact moment it ends. Strange, isn't it? We spend almost all our attention on things starting: the new message, the next episode, the plan for tomorrow. Almost none on things ending. But everything ends. Every sound, every mood, every breath. The last four steps of the breathing discourse turn the whole practice toward that plain fact, and they say it's where freedom is found.
screen: `LISTEN UNTIL THE SOUND STOPS.` → `WE WATCH THINGS START.` → `EVERYTHING ENDS.`

segments.voice: The fourth group of four is about seeing things as they really are. Step thirteen: contemplating impermanence, anicca, I will breathe in and out. Step fourteen: contemplating fading away. Step fifteen: contemplating ceasing. Step sixteen: contemplating letting go, relinquishment. Four words, and each goes a little deeper. Impermanence is the plain observation: this breath is changing. It started, it's moving, it's ending. Fading is seeing that as things change, the pull they have on us can fade too. Ceasing is watching things actually end: the breath, the sound, the thought, gone. And letting go is the hand opening, not because you're forced to but because there's nothing left to cling to. The breath is the perfect teacher for this, because it never stops demonstrating. No in-breath lasts. No out-breath can be kept. You can't save a breath for later. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in four words: "All created things perish." It goes on to say that whoever sees this clearly grows weary of pain, and that this is the way to purity. That sounds bleak to some ears. But practitioners describe the opposite. When you really see that everything changes, you stop gripping so hard, and something relaxes. The bad day will end. The good day will end too, so you'd better enjoy it. And every breath becomes both a beginning and an ending. This is what the discourse calls the fruit of the whole practice: sixteen steps that start with a long breath and end with letting go.
screen: `IMPERMANENCE: THIS BREATH IS CHANGING.` · `FADING: THE PULL FADES TOO.` · `CEASING: WATCH IT END.` · `LETTING GO: THE HAND OPENS.` · then, large: `LET GO.`

segments.voice: Sit, and settle with the breath. Now put your attention on the endings. Notice where each in-breath ends, that small turn at the top. Notice where each out-breath ends, the pause at the bottom. Then widen: notice sounds ending, sensations fading, thoughts dissolving. Nothing to do about it. Just watch things finish. On each out-breath, let something go: a bit of tension, a thought, the need to hold on. The bell holds the time.
Watching change. The last four steps: impermanence, fading, ceasing, and letting go.
Your line: let go. Today, notice one ending: the last sip of coffee, a song finishing, a conversation closing. Let it go. Day one hundred and thirteen.

match.prompt: the last four steps — tap the pairs.

myth: seeing impermanence is meant to make you gloomy
practitioners describe the opposite: when you stop gripping, something relaxes.
the Dhammapada says all created things perish
you can save a breath for later
no in-breath lasts and no out-breath can be kept, which is why the breath is such a good teacher.

fork.setup: you're sitting, and a sound outside suddenly stops. what do the last four steps suggest?
options: ignore it: only the breath matters.
notice the ending, and let it go.
wish the sound would come back.
fork.reveal: steps thirteen to sixteen turn attention to change and ending: every ending is a chance to let go.

original.note: Pali: impermanent; Sanskrit anitya. The first of the three marks of existence.

trapdoor: what you thought: nothing lasts, so why bother.
what it means: seeing change, fading, ending and letting go loosens the grip, and something relaxes.
what a scholar hears: steps thirteen to sixteen form the dhammanupassana tetrad of MN 118: anicca, viraga, nirodha, patinissagga; viraga literally means fading of color, and also dispassion.

sources.ref: MN 118, Anapanasati Sutta: steps thirteen to sixteen

114.title: Counting
114.hook: an old method: count breaths from one to ten, then begin again
114.howItsDone: Counting breaths from one to ten is taught to beginners in many Buddhist traditions, including Theravada, Zen and Tibetan schools, with the instruction to begin again at one whenever the count is lost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, watching change: impermanence, fading, ceasing, letting go. Your line was let go. What ending did you notice? Day one hundred and fourteen.

Here's a confession almost every meditator makes sooner or later. You sit down to watch the breath. Three breaths in, you're planning dinner. Then you're rehearsing an argument. Then you're wondering if you left the stove on. Five minutes later you remember: oh, right, the breath. Sixteen beautiful steps are no use if you can't stay for two. So the old teachers gave beginners something simpler to hold on to. Something any child can do. They count.
screen: `THREE BREATHS, THEN DINNER PLANS.` → `OH, RIGHT, THE BREATH.` → `SOMETHING SIMPLER: COUNT.`

segments.voice: The method is described in the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, as the very first stage of breath meditation for a beginner: ganana, counting. Breathe in, breathe out: one. Breathe in, breathe out: two. Up to ten. Then back to one. And if you lose count, which you will, you also go back to one. The manual is oddly specific about the numbers. Don't stop below five, it says, and don't go beyond ten. Why? If you only count to three or four, the mind feels cramped and restless, like cattle shut in a pen that's too small. If you count past ten, the mind starts paying attention to the numbers instead of the breath. Five to ten is the sweet spot: long enough to settle, short enough to stay with. The manual also says that once the mind can stay with the breath without the counting, you let the counting go. It's scaffolding, not the building. Counting isn't only a Theravada tool. Zen teachers in Japan and elsewhere also teach beginners to count breaths, often to ten, and many Tibetan teachers use counting too. Here's the part that matters most. Losing count isn't failure. It's the practice. Every time you notice you've drifted off to dinner plans and go back to one, that noticing is the muscle getting stronger. Some people get to ten on their first try. Most don't. Many experienced meditators still don't, on a busy day. And every time, the instruction is the same, with no scolding at all. Back to one.
screen: `ONE TO TEN, THEN BEGIN AGAIN.` · `NOT BELOW FIVE, NOT PAST TEN.` · `SCAFFOLDING, NOT THE BUILDING.` · `LOSING COUNT IS THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `BACK TO ONE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath be natural. After each out-breath, count silently: one. Next out-breath: two. Continue to ten, then begin again at one. If you lose track, or catch yourself at fourteen, just smile, and go back to one. No judgment. Try for three rounds, if the time allows; if you only reach three, that's fine too. The counting is a handrail. Keep one hand on it. The bell holds the time.
Counting. An old method for a wandering mind: count breaths from one to ten, and begin again.
Your line: back to one. Today, whenever you lose your place, in a task, a conversation, a plan, say it kindly to yourself: back to one. Day one hundred and fourteen.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: counting; the first stage of breath meditation in the Visuddhimagga.

trapdoor: what you thought: counting sheep for grown-ups.
what it means: a handrail for a wandering mind, dropped once the mind can stay with the breath.
what a scholar hears: Visuddhimagga VIII lists eight stages of breath practice, beginning with ganana (counting) and anubandhana (connection, following the breath).

115.title: The hindrances arrive
115.hook: desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, doubt: five visitors every sitter meets
115.howItsDone: Buddhist meditators learn to recognize the five hindrances when they arise, noting their presence or absence, as the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness describes, before applying any remedy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, counting: one to ten, and back to one. Your line was back to one. How many times did you go back to one today? Day one hundred and fifteen.

By now you've sat with the breath for a couple of weeks, and you've probably met some visitors. The sudden craving for something sweet. A flash of irritation at the neighbor's music. A heavy, sleepy fog. A restless itch to get up and check something. And that quiet voice asking: is this even working? If you've met all five, congratulations. You're completely normal. The Buddha named these visitors twenty-five centuries ago, and every person who has ever sat down to meditate has met them.
screen: `A CRAVING. A FLASH OF IRRITATION.` → `FOG. ITCH. IS THIS WORKING?` → `FIVE VISITORS, COMPLETELY NORMAL.`

segments.voice: Today's word is nivarana, a hindrance, literally a covering, something that blocks the view. The Pali texts list five. One: sensual desire, wanting pleasant things. Two: ill will, irritation, aversion. Three: sloth and torpor, the heavy, dull, sleepy mind. Four: restlessness and worry, the buzzing mind that can't settle, and the nagging regret. Five: doubt, the wobbling mind that can't commit. In a discourse in the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha gives a picture for each, using a bowl of water that you're trying to see your face in. Desire is water mixed with dye: everything gets tinted. Ill will is water boiling. Dullness is water covered in moss. Restlessness is water whipped up by the wind. Doubt is muddy water set in the dark. In every case, you can't see your reflection clearly. And notice: the water itself is fine. It's what's in it, for now. The first thing the tradition teaches about the hindrances is simply to recognize them. In the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, when sensual desire is present, the meditator knows: sensual desire is present. When it's absent, they know it's absent. That's it. Before any remedy, you name it. Why does that help? Because a visitor you've named is no longer running the house. Restlessness you've noticed is just restlessness. Restlessness you haven't noticed becomes you, getting up to check your phone. So think of the hindrances as visitors, not enemies. They knock, they come in, they eventually leave. Your job is to see who's here. Name the visitor.
screen: `NIVARANA: A COVERING.` · `DESIRE, ILL WILL, DULLNESS, RESTLESSNESS, DOUBT.` · `DYED, BOILING, MOSSY, WINDY, MUDDY.` · `FIRST, JUST NAME IT.` · then, large: `NAME THE VISITOR.`

segments.voice: Sit, and settle with the breath. As you sit, watch for visitors. When the mind wanders, before coming back, ask: which one is this? Wanting? Irritation? Dullness? Restlessness? Doubt? Name it softly: ah, restlessness. Then return to the breath. If no visitor is present, notice that too: no restlessness now. Don't fight them, and don't feed them. Just see who's here, and come back. The bell holds the time.
Nivarana. A hindrance, a covering: the five visitors every sitter meets.
Your line: name the visitor. Today, when you feel a craving, irritation, fog, restlessness or doubt, name it silently, before you act. Day one hundred and fifteen.
